name: Freshness clock label
subtitle: a label that clouds as food sits warm

effects.effect: small droplets shrink and feed their material to larger neighbours
small particles scatter a light beam so it shows

effect: small droplets shrink and feed their material to larger neighbours
how: Use-by dates are guesses, so good food is thrown out while food left warm too long gets eaten, and tags that log real temperature cost too much for a pack of fish. This label holds a clear film of tiny oil droplets; the warmer it gets, the faster small droplets feed the big ones (Ostwald ripening), and once they grow large enough to scatter light (Tyndall effect) the window turns milky, just as the food has spent too long warm.
obstacle: Tuning the droplets so their clouding follows how fast each kind of food actually spoils.
why: Labels that show real temperature history cut both food waste and food poisoning.
real: Emulsion-based time-temperature indicators exist in patents and an EU project (emulsion destabilization causing visible change, three-phase emulsions), but none found using Ostwald ripening plus light scattering as the clock.
